text.p: President Bill Clinton, lamenting the use of political insults to sway voters, is using the last days of the presidential campaign to urge Americans to find "common ground" to settle their differences.

With Election Day on Tuesday and most opinion polls showing Clinton with a double-digit lead over Republican rival Bob Dole, the president has been taking the high road as he reaches out to voters across the country.
He planned to use his "common ground" theme in remarks following services Sunday at a black church in Tampa, which neighbours St. Petersburg -- a community torn by racial rioting earlier this month.
"I believe we can find common ground," Clinton told crowds Saturday as he outlined his differences with Republicans.

After his remarks at St. Paul's AME Church, Clinton was expected to meet with St. Petersburg Mayor David Fischer to discuss the death of 18-year-old TyRon Lewis, a black, who was shot and killed earlier this month by two white police officers who stopped him for speeding.
The incident touched off rioting and has prompted the NAACP and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to call for an investigation by outside authorities.
Clinton has honed his skills when it comes to delivering messages about national healing and reminding Americans of the nation's goal to meld their ethnic diversity into a united national spirit.

Although polling conducted for Reuters shows a narrowing in Clinton's lead over Dole, Clinton campaign officials insisted that their extensive polling shows the incumbent with a steady 12 to 15 percentage point lead.
The proof of their confidence can be seen in the states Clinton has chosen to take his message during the final days before Tuesday's election.

Four years ago Clinton ignored Florida as a lost cause, but now he and Vice President Al Gore have been campaigning in the state -- convinced they can become the first Democratic ticket to win the state since Jimmy Carter and Walter Mondale in 1976.

On Saturday, Clinton's schedule included appearances in Texas and Louisiana, usually the domain of Republican candidates -- as well as his home state of Arkansas, to help the struggling Senate campaign of fellow Democrat Winston Bryant.
In addition to Florida, Clinton's schedule Sunday included New Jersey, Massachusetts, Maine and New Hampshire, where many of the stops are more designed to help congressional candidates than himself.

Clinton has been trying to take the high ground in his campaign appearances, ignoring the increasing attacks on his character by Republicans to opt for a message that says "the politics of division yields only division and gridlock."
"The search for common ground yields solutions and progress and a future worthy of our past," he said in his weekly radio address to the nation.
